title: Property is not God's gift to Adam—it is an agreement humans later reached
dek: Grotius argues that in the state of nature, humans have only the right to use things, not to possess them; ownership arises from human agreement, not from God's gift to Adam's descendants.
why: If you want to understand how taken-for-granted concepts like ‘freedom of the seas’ and ‘international law’ were first argued into existence and how they served concrete business interests, this episode traces the complete chain.
who: Readers of law and philosophy interested in property theory, natural law tradition, and the origins of early international law—and anyone wanting to see how academic theory serves commercial interests.
skip: 0:00-4:07 You can skip Grotius's escape and biographical sections; jump straight to the property theory at 5:11.

points.h: Freedom of the seas is ultimately a claim about property
points.body: Grotius opposed any state or company asserting sovereignty over the ocean—not for political reasons, but on property grounds: no one can own any part of the sea, so merchant ships have the right to trade freely through it. The argument sounds like a claim about maritime freedom, but to understand it you must first grasp Grotius's answer to a more fundamental question: why does property exist at all?

points.h: Natural law holds even without God
points.body: Grotius held that all law derives from some legislator's will, and the legislator of natural law is of course God. But he boldly posed a thought experiment: even if God did not exist, natural law would still be self-evident and binding for us. God is the source of this law, but once created, humans can discover its rules simply by studying nature itself.

points.h: Nature gives us use alone, not possession
points.body: Grotius rejected the prevailing view that property rights trace back to Adam and Eve and pass down through inheritance. In the state of nature, he argued, humans have only the right to use things, not to possess them. This distinction echoes a thirteenth-century Franciscan debate over vows of poverty: monks claimed the library books and stores' food did not belong to them—they were merely using them.

points.h: Possession ends the moment continuous use stops
points.body: Drawing on Cicero's example, Grotius compared this right of use to finding a seat in a theater—whoever sits down first has the right to it until the performance ends. The same rule applied to enclosure and cultivation: if someone fenced off a meadow to farm it, others should let him use it. But possession was not permanent. Once use stopped—say, to study croissant-making in France for a year—your neighbor could claim the land was no longer yours.

points.h: The hungry retain a legal right to steal bread
points.body: Grotius held that even after humans later reached agreement through the Law of Nations and established a true system of ownership, the right of necessity from the state of nature was always retained: in life-or-death emergencies, anyone has the right to use another's things to survive, and must compensate afterward if able. No one would agree to surrender this right, so we can be certain such an agreement was never truly made.

points.h: Water is too fluid ever to be possessed
points.body: Grotius argued that the ocean could never be possessed in part or in whole by anyone, since—except for rivers and narrow straits—water was too ‘fluid’ to be enclosed or worked to demonstrate occupation as land could be. The deeper reason: God distributed resources unevenly across the earth precisely to force humans to trade with each other, and the boundless sea ensures that this common right to use it can never be overridden by local claims of possession.

points.h: Latitude and longitude bind the seas as fences do land
points.body: Grotius's argument was rebutted by jurist William Welwod, Portuguese friar Serafim Freitas, and Englishman John Selden. They pointed out that while you cannot build a fence in the middle of the Atlantic, lines of latitude and longitude draw boundaries just as well—the 1494 Treaty of Tordesillas used a meridian to divide the world between Spain and Portugal. They also countered that land changes too, but that does not prevent land from being owned, so why should water be different?

points.h: This theory began as a Dutch East India Company brief
points.body: Grotius's argument for freedom of the seas was originally part of a longer manuscript he drafted for the Dutch East India Company (VOC) and published separately for diplomatic reasons. When the Dutch later wanted to establish a monopoly on eastern trade themselves, this free-trade argument became a weapon against them—the English directly used Grotius's own words to rebut him, spurring him to write a second major work, De Jure Belli ac Pacis, to revise his position.
